extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in evolutionary biology, genetics, and quantitative heredity
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation and quantitative rules for bi-parental inheritance, mid-parent and mid-ancestor concepts, the law of ancestral heredity, coefficients of heredity (direct and collateral), cross-heredity, and the effect of selection in establishing breeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of coefficients of heredity
rubrics_metrics.description: The correlation between the father's and the son's organs is the coefficient of paternal heredity; the correlation between the mother's and the son's organs is the coefficient of maternal heredity; the correlation between the father's and mother's organs is the intensity of assortative mating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measured correlations between parent and offspring pairs (and between mates) as fundamental parameters when computing regressions, partial regression coefficients, and inheritance intensities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bi-parental regression equation (two-parent contribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: When deviations from the type are small, the type of the son's array must consist of two terms proportional to the deviations of the father and mother: μ3 = c1 × μ1 + c2 × μ2, where c1 and c2 are numerical constants (partial regression coefficients) determined by correlations and variabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute c1 and c2 (partial regression coefficients) from the correlations and standard-deviations of the three organs; these involve no further assumptions beyond those for uni-parental inheritance. The algebra leads to explicit formulae (given in the text) relating c1, c2 to the correlation coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mid-parent concept and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace the male and female parents by a single artificial parent (the mid-parent) by 'reducing the female organ to its male equivalent' using the ratio of male to female variability and then taking the mean of the paternal and maternal male-equivalent organs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: compute the female's male-equivalent deviation by multiplying by (σ_male / σ_female), then average with the father's value to get the mid-parent. Mid-parent has variability S = sqrt((σ1^2 + σ2^2)/2) and correlation with offspring R = r_male * sqrt( (1 + r_female) / (1 + r_male) ) (formulae appear in text). The mid-parent formalism simplifies bi-parental inheritance to uni-parental regression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of mating system on variability and correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: Special cases: (i) perfect assortative mating (self-fertilisation) gives β = 1, mid-parent variability equals individual parent and R = r1; (ii) pangamic mating (random mating) leads to specific reductions in mid-parent variability and different R values (numerical examples given: S = 0.707σ, R = 0.4242 if r = 0.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appropriate mating assumptions (assortative, pangamic, selfing) to choose the correct formulas for mid-parent variability and correlation; numerical examples illustrate how selecting one vs both parents affects reduction in population variability (~5% vs ~10%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Asexual/parthenogenetic reproduction properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations (from daphnia and other parthenogenetic cases): (i) an asexual individual does not produce a facsimile of itself and offspring variability is not immensely reduced below race variability; (ii) asexually produced offspring exhibit regression toward the race type like sexually produced offspring; (iii) the asexual mother often represents the mid-parent (empirical correlations similar to mid-parent values).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret parthenogenetic mother-offspring correlations (e.g., correlation ≈ .466, regression ≈ .619) in light of mid-parent expectations (.424 and .600) — differences may be due to environment or growth changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability is not produced by bi-parental inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusion (a): Variability is not a product of bi-parental inheritance — the individual contains a bathmic law of growth producing variability which is about 80–90% of racial variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect individual variability to be only slightly less than racial variability based on empirical data (examples: poppies, ash leaflets). This counters arguments that sexual reproduction is the main source of variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex does not produce greater variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusion (V): Whatever the physiological function of sex, it is not the production of greater variability; the variability of mid-parents is less than that of single parents and is closely allied to parthenogenetic mothers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attribute large increases in variability to sexual reproduction per se; analyze variability using mid-parent framework and empirical measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on reduction of variability by selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusion (e): No amount of selection seems capable of reducing variability beyond some 10 to 11 percent (theoretical maximum limit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use algebraic results and tables to show selection's limited effect on reducing racial variability; typical computed values and tables in text illustrate this limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heredity as law explaining regression (change of type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusion (f): Heredity is the law which accounts for the change of type between parent and offspring (regression toward the race type); heredity is consistent with diverse degrees of racial variability and not inversely related to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret regression and offspring variability via formulae for regression and variability (pp. 397 and 401 referenced) rather than assuming heredity scales simply with overall variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of inheritance rates across organs (empirical tendency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusion (g): From a considerable number of measurements, there is an approach (though not exact) to the law that all organs and characters in all forms of life are inherited at the same rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If true, heredity must precede evolution; deviations may be due to environment or sexual selection modifications but do not imply heredity is produced by evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of ancestral heredity (geometrical contribution rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each parent contributes on average one-quarter (0.5^2), each grandparent one-sixteenth (0.5^4), etc.; more generally contributions of successive ancestral generations form a geometrical series (coefficients y1, y2,...), leading to the law of ancestral heredity determining offspring type from ancestral deviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express offspring type h as a weighted sum of ancestral mid-parent deviations H1,H2,... with weights forming a geometric series; introduce constants a and t (the constant of heredity) so that for stable race h = y a/(1-a) etc. The constant t summarizes total hereditary influence; deviations from unity represent 'taxing' of ancestral contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative coefficients of heredity (direct line and collateral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical tables of correlation coefficients for direct-line relatives (parent, grandparent, great-grandparent, etc.) and collateral relatives (brothers, uncle & nephew, cousins, etc.) are provided under blended inheritance/pangamic mating (e.g., parent ≈ .4000, grandparent .1500, brother .4000, uncle-nephew .1500, first cousins .0750, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these theoretical coefficients (and variants when the constant t differs, e.g., t=2.35) as baseline expectations to compare with empirical measurements; differences indicate effects of mating system, selection, or non-pangamic mating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for cross heredity (between different characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross heredity: multiply the coefficient of direct heredity by the organic correlation between the two characters to obtain the coefficient of cross heredity (e.g., inheritance from father's stature to son's forearm equals direct heredity coefficient times correlation between stature and forearm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure organic correlations between characters and apply multiplicative rule to predict cross-character relatedness; empirical tests (ongoing measurements) can validate this law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of selection to establish breeds and change type over generations
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection over successive generations can permanently modify types: tables show fraction of selected deviation retained after 1,2,3,... generations (e.g., after 1 gen = .5, after 2 = .75, after 3 = .875, ... tending to 1), while variability of selected population relative to racial variability approaches a limiting reduction (~.8944).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for ancestry when predicting response to selection—regression is reduced if ancestry is also selected; selection may lead stock to 'breed true' to a high fraction of selected character after several generations (numerical tables and formulas provided). If selection is suspended, offspring breed true to the fraction achieved. Use the provided algebraic expressions and tables for pedigree stock and for cases where earlier mid-parents are unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedigree-stock constants and expected retention
rubrics_metrics.description: For pedigree or recorded-stock selection, constants e1, e2,... characterize the ratio of final to selected type given number of generations of record; tables of these constants show limiting values (e.g., infinite generations give retention of .5, .25, .125, ... for successive pedigree depths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'TABLE OF PEDIGREE STOCK' constants to estimate how much of an originally selected character will remain in final stock depending on how many generations of recorded selection are available; compare to the theoretical infinite-record limits.
